summary: Looks at a deployment problem with TLS-based EAP methods: large certificates and long certificate chains, combined with authenticators that drop an EAP session after only 40 to 50 round trips. The document describes the problem in detail and the potential solutions. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A very long ID card takes so many small handovers that the doorman gives up. This explains how to make it shorter.

questions: eap session dropped after many round trips
why does eap-tls fail with large certificates
how many round trips before an access point drops eap
how to shrink eap-tls certificate chains
subtitle: Why big certificate chains break Wi-Fi and wired logins that use EAP-TLS, and the ways to shrink or work around them.

tldr.problem: Large certificates and long chains in TLS-based EAP methods must be split into many small packets, and some authenticators drop an EAP session after 40 to 50 round trips.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys fixes: smaller certificates and shorter chains, TLS and EAP-TLS changes such as certificate compression or caching, and raising the round trip limit in authenticators.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational guide, not a new protocol. Many of the solutions require TLS 1.3.

today: RFC 9191 is an Informational document. The unit metadata shows nothing obsoleting or updating it, so it stands as the guidance on large certificates in TLS-based EAP methods.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
EAP-TLS relies on TLS to provide strong mutual authentication with certificates and is widely deployed for network access authentication. Unlike web TLS, where usually only the server is authenticated, EAP-TLS typically authenticates both the EAP peer and the EAP server, and peers often have longer chains because they follow organizational hierarchies.

EAP implementations can assume a lower-layer MTU of at least 1020 octets, and typical EAP fragment size is 1020 to 1500 octets, so the exchange is split into many packets. Some authenticators (an access point, for example) drop an EAP session that has not finished after 40 to 50 round trips, so a peer with valid credentials can fail to get network access. RADIUS can generally carry only about 4000 octets of EAP in one message.
sections.eli5: The messages must travel in small envelopes. A long certificate needs so many envelopes that the gatekeeper stops waiting and sends you away.

sections.title: What Makes Certificates Big
sections.content:
A certificate can be large because of a long Subject Alternative Name field, long public key and signature fields, multiple OIDs that indicate permitted uses, or multiple organization naming fields for a user's group memberships. A chain can commonly have 2 to 6 intermediate certificates between the end-entity certificate and the trust anchor.

Because many access points drop sessions after 40 to 50 round trips, a chain larger than about 60 kilobytes cannot complete in most deployments. Post-quantum cryptography may make this worse: the RFC gives approximately 1000 bytes for lattice-based public keys and approximately 2000 bytes for signatures.
sections.eli5: Every extra detail written on the ID card makes it longer. Long chains of vouching letters make it longer still.

sections.title: Fix 1: Smaller Certificates and Chains
sections.content:
Using elliptic curve cryptography shrinks keys and signatures. At a 128-bit security level the RFC gives about 384 bytes for an RSA public key against 32 to 64 bytes for ECC, and 384 bytes for an RSA signature against 64 bytes for ECDSA or EdDSA. Certificate guidelines include shallower distinguished names, careful choice of certificate policies, short names and URLs, only the extensions needed, and trimmed intermediate certificates.

Endpoints can omit certificates the other side already has. With TLS 1.3, all certificates that specify a known trust anchor may be omitted; with TLS 1.2 or earlier, only the self-signed root may be omitted. The omitted certificates must be pre-distributed independently. Chains SHOULD NOT contain more than 4 intermediate certificates. As a rough check, divide the total size of the peer and server chains in bytes by 1020; if the result exceeds 50, expect failures with many common authenticators.
sections.eli5: Write less on the card, use a smaller and cleverer kind of lock, and do not bother carrying letters the gatekeeper already has.

sections.title: Fix 2: Changing TLS and EAP-TLS Code
sections.content:
Several TLS mechanisms can cut what is sent. The client_certificate_url extension lets a client send URLs instead of its chain. The Cached Information Extension lets a server skip certificates the client cached in an earlier full handshake, though that needs one successful full handshake first. Certificate compression for TLS 1.3 compresses certificates and chains during full handshakes, but works only with TLS 1.3 and higher.

Other options are compact TLS 1.3 (cTLS), a proposal to let a client tell the server it already has the intermediates, the Authority Information Access extension (a pointer to the issuer instead of the full certificate, which cannot be used for the server certificate because peers usually lack network access before authentication), raw public keys (much smaller, but needing an out-of-band way to bind key and identity), and early work on CBOR-encoded certificates.
sections.eli5: Other tricks let the two sides say, I already know that one, or squash the letters flat before sending, or swap the big ID card for a simple key that was agreed beforehand.

sections.title: Fix 3: Updating Authenticators
sections.content:
Authenticators have legitimate reasons to limit packets or round trips: to avoid an infinite loop of acknowledgements between peer and server, to stop unauthenticated devices using EAP as a bulk data channel, and to prevent denial-of-service attacks. But updating millions of deployed access points and switches is often not realistic, so the RFC calls the EAP infrastructure ossified for the time being.

Vendors making new authenticators should consider allowing 100 round trips before denying authentication, and administrators should make sure the 100 round-trip limit is not exceeded in practice.
sections.eli5: The best fix is a more patient doorman, but old doormen are hard to replace. New ones should wait up to 100 handovers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC notes that updating to TLS 1.3 lets implementations omit all certificates with a trust anchor known by the other side, and also brings improved security, privacy and reduced latency for EAP-TLS. Security considerations for certificate compression are in RFC 8879, and the security considerations of the other referenced documents apply when they are used. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Upgrading to the newer TLS helps with size and also makes things safer. Each trick you borrow brings its own safety notes.
